idiom_name: nested functions and arrow closures over the method's locals
implementation_notes: Every function created inside the method is a closure over its lexical environment (MDN), so the steps become nested function declarations or arrow functions that read and write the same let/const bindings; no class is needed and the environment dies with the call. The class form with #private fields remains the right choice when the algorithm must be a reusable, testable unit, be passed around as a value, or be serialized - and note that private fields give per-class hard privacy for an instance, not a closure over one invocation.
pitfalls: A closure returned from the method keeps the whole captured environment alive; closing over a large object or a DOM node pins it for as long as the function is reachable.
Capture is by binding, not by value: a var (or a let read after reassignment) makes every closure observe the later value, which is the classic loop-variable bug.
Nested function expressions have their own this; use arrow functions or bind the receiver explicitly when a step needs this.
